error_modes.label: DEVIATION FROM TURNING POINTS (radius)
error_modes.source: specific:DEVIATION FROM TURNING POINTS* (radius in NM)

texts.0: SP, due to map reading based on a single ground feature instead of a pattern of features, did not overfly the turning points within the required radius. SP passed the second turning point about 4 NM abeam and the third about 5 NM abeam, well beyond the 2 NM radius, and the ground track diverged progressively from the planned leg. IP had to take over the navigation and direct SP back onto the planned track before the next leg could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to an early acceptance of a road junction that resembled the briefed feature, did not overfly the turning points within the tighter radius. SP passed the turning points about 2 NM abeam, at the outer limit of the standard, and repositioned onto the planned track only after IP pointed out the correct feature over the intercom. Each subsequent turning point required the same verbal prompting to keep the deviation from growing further.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading held without allowance for the reported wind on the first leg, initially tracked about 1.7 NM to the right of the planned turning point. SP compared the terrain with the chart, identified the offset while still inbound and applied a correction that placed the aircraft over the following turning points inside the radius. No IP input was required at any stage of the correction.
texts.3: SP overflew every turning point within a radius of 1 NM, positively identifying each one against the chart before commencing the turn. Track corrections were small and applied early, so no leg required a repositioning maneuver. Navigation continued from each turning point without any regain of track.
texts.4: SP overflew each turning point practically overhead, with the aircraft crossing the selected features rather than passing abeam of them. Wind corrections were computed and applied on every leg, so the lateral deviation remained negligible throughout the route. Chart and terrain agreed at every point of the navigation.
texts.marginal: SP overflew the turning points within standards, but the offset was consistently on the same side of track and grew toward 1 NM by the final legs. The trend is a wind correction that is applied once at the start of the navigation and is not revised as the actual drift becomes apparent. SP is expected to reassess drift on each leg and keep the turning points overhead rather than at the edge of the acceptable radius.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the correct feature over the intercom and directing the reposition onto track, SP flew the heading given back toward the planned turning point. Comparing the terrain with the chart to identify an offset independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the correction still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin comparing the terrain with the chart before the IP names the feature, with the IP still confirming it, before an independent correction is required.
texts_at.1: SP repositioned onto the planned track with the turning point overflown at about 1.8 NM from the reference, correcting after the terrain comparison identified the offset. The wide pass traced to a heading held without allowance for the reported wind on the first leg of the route. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to apply the reported wind to the heading before the first leg rather than after the first turning point shows the error.
texts_at.2: SP compared the terrain with the chart and closed the offset, overflying the turning point at about 1.4 NM from the reference before the following point. The wide pass traced to a heading that had not yet been corrected for the actual wind encountered on the leg. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compare the actual drift against the reported wind by the first turning point, not only after it.
texts_at.3: SP overflew the turning point within about 0.6 NM of the reference, applying track corrections early and in the correct direction. The small residual came from a wind correction that was reassessed a leg later than the earliest point it could have been. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reassess the drift correction one leg earlier so the residual is removed by the following point.

texts_above.1: SP flew the heading given by the IP and repositioned onto the planned track, overflying the turning point at about 1.8 NM from the reference. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP compared the terrain with the chart and closed the developing offset, overflying the turning point at about 1.3 NM from the reference. Reassessing the wind correction the moment the first leg begins, rather than after the first point, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good turning point overflight technique.
texts_above.3: SP overflew every turning point within a radius of about 0.6 NM, applying small corrections early and in the correct direction on every leg. The technique is already sound; only the first leg of the route still calls for the wind correction to be confirmed a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good drift correction consistency.
texts_above.4: SP overflew each turning point practically overhead, with the lateral deviation inside about 0.2 NM on every leg of the route. The only refinement available was to log the wind correction applied on each leg for the debrief, since the overflight itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent turning point precision.

texts.0: SP, due to a leg flown at an airspeed well below the planned one without any recomputation, did not arrive at the turning points at the calculated times. Arrival at the second turning point was about 2 minutes late and at the third about 2 minutes 30 seconds late, far beyond the 60 second tolerance. IP had to compute the required groundspeed and direct the power setting in order to restore the timing of the remaining legs.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed start of the leg timing after the turn was completed, arrived at the turning points about 60 seconds outside the calculated times, at the limit of the standard. SP adjusted the airspeed only after IP asked for the running time on the leg, and the same delay reappeared on the following leg. The timing was contained within the standard solely through repeated verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed check made late in the first leg, initially built an error of about 50 seconds against the calculated arrival time. SP identified the discrepancy at the midpoint of the leg, computed the required correction and adjusted the airspeed so that the following turning points were crossed within 30 seconds of the plan. No IP intervention was needed to recover the timing.
texts.3: SP arrived at each turning point within 30 seconds of the calculated time, starting and stopping the leg timing at the correct points. Groundspeed was checked early on every leg and small airspeed adjustments were applied before the error could accumulate. Timing on all turning points remained inside the tighter criterion.
texts.4: SP arrived at every turning point within a few seconds of the calculated time, with the timing error never allowed to build on any leg. Groundspeed was recomputed at each half-leg checkpoint and the airspeed corrections applied were small and anticipatory. Deviations from the planned arrival times were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the turning points within standards, but the arrival times were consistently early and the error grew from leg to leg toward the 30 second figure. The trend is an airspeed flown above the planned one without an accompanying check of the effect on leg timing. SP is expected to check groundspeed against the plan early in each leg and to correct the airspeed while the timing error is still small.

texts_at.0: With the IP computing the required groundspeed and directing the power setting, SP applied the airspeed given to restore the leg timing. Computing the groundspeed correction from the running time independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the airspeed adjustment still depends on the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin stating the running time against the plan before the IP computes the correction, with the IP still directing the power setting, before an independent correction is required.
texts_at.1: SP adjusted the airspeed and closed the arrival time to about 55 seconds from the calculated figure before the following point. The late correction traced to a groundspeed check started after the leg was already under way rather than early in it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the groundspeed check early in every leg so the correction is available before the arrival time is affected.
texts_at.2: SP computed the correction and adjusted the airspeed, holding the arrival time to about 40 seconds from the calculated figure. The delay traced to a groundspeed check made later in the leg than the technique calls for. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move the groundspeed check earlier in the leg so the correction has more of the leg remaining to take effect.
texts_at.3: SP arrived at the turning point within about 18 seconds of the calculated time, checking groundspeed early and applying small airspeed adjustments. The small residual came from a check completed a few seconds later than the earliest point on the leg. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the groundspeed check a few seconds earlier on the leg so the arrival time comes in closer to the calculated figure.

texts_above.1: SP applied the airspeed directed by the IP and closed the arrival time to within about 55 seconds of the calculated figure, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked groundspeed early on the leg and adjusted airspeed before the error could grow, holding the arrival time to about 40 seconds of the calculated figure. Moving that groundspeed check a little earlier still, right after roll-out, would leave an even smaller correction to apply. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound leg timing technique.
texts_above.3: SP arrived at the turning point within about 18 seconds of the calculated time on every leg, checking groundspeed early and applying small airspeed adjustments before any error could accumulate. The technique is already sound; only the shortest legs would still call for the groundspeed check to start a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed leg timing management.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at every turning point within a few seconds of the calculated time, with the timing error never allowed to build on any leg. The only refinement available was to log the groundspeed figure used on each leg for the debrief, since the timing itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional leg timing precision.

texts.0: SP, due to timing errors on successive legs that were never corrected once identified, did not control the total duration of the navigation flight. The route was completed about 3 minutes later than the planned total time, well beyond the 90 second tolerance, and the recovery time no longer matched the flight plan. IP had to reassign the airspeed and delete a portion of the final leg in order to recover the sortie within the fuel available.
texts.1: SP, due to individual leg errors that were treated in isolation rather than against the running total, completed the navigation about 90 seconds off the planned total time, at the limit of the standard. SP began adjusting the airspeed only after IP asked for the accumulated time against the plan. The total time was kept inside the standard only because of that prompting on the last leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a slower than planned groundspeed on the first two legs, accumulated an error of about 70 seconds against the planned total time. SP recognized the accumulation while abeam the third turning point, increased the airspeed for the remaining legs and completed the navigation within 45 seconds of the plan. The correction was computed and applied without IP input.
texts.3: SP completed the navigation within 45 seconds of the planned total time, monitoring the accumulated time against the plan at each turning point. Where a leg produced a small error, SP absorbed it on the following leg rather than carrying it forward. The total duration of the flight matched the mission plan.
texts.4: SP completed the navigation within a few seconds of the planned total time, with the running total kept aligned with the plan throughout the route. Every leg error was identified at the turning point and absorbed immediately, so nothing accumulated toward the end of the navigation. The deviation on total time was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the navigation within standards, but the accumulated error reached the 45 second figure and was only absorbed on the last leg. The trend is a total time that is checked at the end of the route rather than maintained at each turning point. SP is expected to compare the running total against the plan at every turning point and to spread the correction over the remaining legs.

texts_at.0: With the IP reassigning the airspeed and stating the accumulated time against the plan, SP flew the airspeed given for the remaining legs. Comparing the running total against the plan independently, rather than tracking each leg error in isolation, has not yet been asked of SP, so total time control still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin stating the running total at each turning point before the IP asks for it, before an independent correction is required.
texts_at.1: SP increased the airspeed for the remaining legs and completed the navigation about 82 seconds off the planned total time. The accumulation traced to individual leg errors that were tracked separately rather than against the running total early in the route. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compare the running total against the plan at every turning point from the first leg, not only near the end of the route.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the accumulation and increased the airspeed for the remaining legs, completing the navigation within about 62 seconds of the planned total time. The build-up traced to a slower than planned groundspeed on the first two legs that was not checked against the running total. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to check the running total against the plan after every leg, including the first two, so a slow start is caught early.
texts_at.3: SP completed the navigation within about 27 seconds of the planned total time, monitoring the accumulated time against the plan at each turning point. The small residual came from a leg error absorbed a turning point later than the earliest point it could have been. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to absorb a small leg error on the very next leg rather than carrying it forward one further.

texts_above.1: SP flew the airspeed given by the IP for the remaining legs and completed the navigation about 82 seconds off the planned total time. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP monitored the accumulated time against the plan at each turning point and increased airspeed before the error could grow, completing the navigation within about 62 seconds of the planned total time. Absorbing a small leg error on the very next leg, rather than one further on, would tighten that margin still further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid total time management.
texts_above.3: SP completed the navigation within about 27 seconds of the planned total time, monitoring the accumulated time against the plan at every turning point and absorbing each small error on the following leg. The technique is already sound; only the first two legs of the route still call for the running total to be checked a touch earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate total time management.
texts_above.4: SP completed the navigation within a few seconds of the planned total time, with the running total kept aligned with the plan throughout the route. The only refinement available was to log the running total at each turning point for the debrief, since the timing itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding total time control.

error_modes.label: IDENTIFICATION OF TURNING POINTS AGAINST THE CHART

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to the planned route, did not recognize the turning points confidently. SP misidentified the second turning point, called a lake that was not the briefed feature and continued on a heading that belonged to a different leg. IP had to identify the correct feature, state the aircraft position and reestablish the navigation for SP.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of a terrain feature that was available in the mission planning material, recognized the turning points only with hesitation. SP overflew the feature without calling it and identified it as the turning point only after IP asked what was below the aircraft. Recognition of the remaining points continued to depend on the same prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial fixation on a single linear feature instead of the briefed pattern of features, was slow to recognize the third turning point. SP widened the visual search, cross-checked two secondary features against the chart and identified the point positively while still able to turn on the planned track. The remaining turning points were recognized without hesitation and without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP recognized all turning points confidently, identifying each one against the chart before reaching it and announcing it in good time. The visual search was based on a pattern of features rather than a single object, so no point was confused with a similar one. Navigation proceeded from each recognized point without doubt about the aircraft position.
texts.4: SP recognized every turning point well in advance, calling each feature and its confirming secondary features while still inbound on the leg. Position awareness along the route was continuous and SP was able to state the aircraft position relative to the plan at any moment. Recognition was immediate and unambiguous at every point.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the turning points within standards, but the identification was made only overhead the feature and rested on one object at a time. The trend is a visual search that starts too late to allow a confirmation before the turn. SP is expected to begin identifying the next turning point early in the leg and to confirm it with secondary features before reaching it.

texts_at.0: With the IP identifying the correct feature and stating the aircraft position, SP continued the leg on the heading confirmed. Recognizing turning points from a pattern of features independently has not yet been asked of SP, so recognition still depends on the IP's call at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin naming one feature of the pattern before the IP identifies the point, with the IP still confirming it, before an independent recognition is required.
texts_at.1: SP identified the turning point from the pattern of features with the overflight at about 1.8 NM from the reference before the picture was confirmed. The hesitation traced to a terrain feature that had been available in the mission planning material but was not reviewed again before the leg. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the planning material for each turning point again shortly before the leg, not only during the original planning.
texts_at.2: SP widened the visual search and cross-checked two secondary features, overflying the point at about 1.4 NM from the reference. The initial fixation traced to a single linear feature being taken as sufficient before the briefed pattern of features was checked. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check the briefed pattern of features before settling on a single one as the turning point.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the turning point confidently and overflew it within about 0.6 NM of the reference. The small residual came from a secondary feature confirmed a moment later than the primary one on the leg with the least distinctive terrain. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the secondary feature in the same glance as the primary one on the least distinctive legs.

texts_above.1: SP continued the leg on the feature identified by the IP, overflying the turning point at about 1.8 NM from the reference once the position was confirmed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP widened the visual search early and cross-checked the briefed pattern of features, overflying the turning point at about 1.3 NM from the reference. Reviewing the planning material again shortly before the leg, rather than relying on the original planning alone, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady turning point identification.
texts_above.3: SP recognized every turning point confidently, identifying each one against the chart before reaching it and overflying it within about 0.6 NM. The technique is already sound; only the least distinctive terrain still calls for the secondary feature to be confirmed a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed turning point recognition.
texts_above.4: SP recognized every turning point well in advance, calling each feature and its confirming secondary features while still inbound, with the overflight held inside about 0.2 NM. The only refinement available was to log the confirming feature used for each point for the debrief, since the recognition itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary turning point recognition.

error_modes.label: TIMELY TURN AND ROLLOUT ON THE NEXT HEADING

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started only after the turning point had been left well behind, did not turn to the next heading timely. SP rolled out about 20 degrees off the planned heading and did not correct it, so the following leg was flown displaced from the planned track from the start. IP had to command the corrected heading and supervise the regain of the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn commenced without the next heading having been selected in advance, turned late toward the next heading and rolled out about 12 degrees off. SP corrected the heading only after IP stated the planned figure over the intercom. The same late selection and prompted correction were repeated at the following turning point.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle chosen without allowance for the size of the heading change, initially rolled out about 8 degrees short of the planned heading. SP compared the heading with the planned one immediately after rollout, applied the correction within a few seconds and continued the leg on track. Subsequent turns were flown onto the planned heading without deviation and without IP input.
texts.3: SP turned to the next heading timely at each turning point, with the next heading already known before the turn was commenced. Rollout was on the planned heading and the new leg was flown on track from the outset. No heading correction was required after any of the turns.
texts.4: SP commenced each turn precisely at the turning point and rolled out exactly on the planned heading, with the bank angle selected to suit the size of every heading change. The next heading and leg time were set up before the point was reached, so the transition between legs was seamless. Heading deviations after rollout were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP turned to the next headings within standards, but the turns were commenced slightly late and the rollouts were consistently a few degrees short of the planned figure. The trend is a turn that begins as a reaction to passing the feature rather than as a planned action. SP is expected to preset the next heading and to anticipate the turn so that rollout occurs on the planned heading.

texts_at.0: With the IP stating the planned heading over the intercom, SP corrected onto the heading given once it was called. Selecting and presetting the next heading before starting the turn independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the rollout heading still depends on the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin naming the next heading before the IP states it, with the IP still confirming the figure, before an independent selection is required.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the heading onto the planned course with the resulting overflight at about 1.8 NM from the next reference before the correction closed. The late rollout traced to the next heading not having been selected before the turn was commenced. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to select and preset the next heading before starting the turn on every turning point.
texts_at.2: SP compared the heading with the planned figure immediately after rollout, holding the following overflight to about 1.4 NM from the reference. The short rollout traced to a bank angle chosen without allowance for the size of the heading change required. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size the bank angle to the heading change required before starting the turn, not adjust it once rolling.
texts_at.3: SP turned to the next heading timely and rolled out on the planned figure, holding the following overflight within about 0.6 NM. The small residual came from a bank angle set a touch light for the size of the heading change on one turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to match the bank angle to the size of the heading change a little more closely on the next repetition.

texts_above.1: SP corrected onto the heading stated by the IP, overflying the following turning point at about 1.8 NM from the reference before the correction closed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP selected the next heading before starting the turn and rolled out with only a small residual, holding the following overflight to about 1.3 NM from the reference. Sizing the bank angle to the heading change before starting the turn, rather than adjusting it once rolling, would remove even that residual. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable turn and rollout technique.
texts_above.3: SP turned to the next heading timely at every turning point, with the next heading already known before the turn was commenced, holding the overflight within about 0.6 NM. The technique is already sound; only the largest heading changes still call for the bank angle to be sized a touch more precisely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise turn and rollout technique.
texts_above.4: SP commenced each turn precisely at the turning point and rolled out exactly on the planned heading, holding the overflight inside about 0.2 NM on every turn. The only refinement available was to log the bank angle used for each heading change for the debrief, since the turn itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding turn and rollout precision.

error_modes.label: TURNING POINT OBSCURED BY CLOUD - TIMED TURN

texts.0: SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the actual conditions had changed, did not turn to the next point at the completion of the leg time when the turning point was covered by clouds. SP continued straight ahead searching visually for the obscured feature and overflew the point by more than 3 minutes of flight. IP had to command the turn and reconstruct the remaining route timing.
texts.1: SP, due to an aircraft position that had diverged from the mental model without being reassessed, did not turn at the completion of the leg time over the cloud covered turning point. SP started the turn about 60 seconds late, after IP asked what the leg time was showing. The dependence on that prompting persisted when the following point was also obscured.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial decision to continue searching for the obscured feature through a gap in the cloud, allowed about 40 seconds to pass beyond the completion of the leg time. SP then referred to the leg timing, accepted it as the primary reference and turned onto the next heading before the error could affect the following leg. The decision and the turn were made without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP turned to the next point at the completion of the leg time whenever the turning point was covered by clouds, without waiting for a visual identification that was not available. The turn was flown onto the preplanned heading and the timing of the following leg was started correctly. Navigation continued unaffected by the cloud cover.
texts.4: SP anticipated the cloud covered turning point, briefed the transition to timed navigation before reaching it and turned exactly at the completion of the leg time. The following leg was flown on the planned heading and the visual navigation was resumed at the first feature that became available. The interruption of the visual navigation produced negligible error.
texts.marginal: SP turned at the completion of the leg time as required, but the decision to abandon the visual search was taken only in the last seconds before the leg time expired. The trend is a late acceptance of timing as the primary reference when the feature is not visible. SP is expected to decide on the timed turn as soon as the turning point is assessed as obscured, rather than at the expiry of the leg time.

texts_at.0: With the IP asking what the leg time was showing and directing the turn, SP turned onto the next heading once the call was made. Accepting the leg timing as the primary reference over a visual search independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the timed turn decision still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin stating the leg time out loud as the turning point is assessed obscured, before the IP asks for it, before an independent decision is required.
texts_at.1: SP turned onto the next heading with the decision reached about 55 seconds beyond the completion of the leg time. The delay traced to the aircraft position having diverged from the mental model without being reassessed against the leg timing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reassess the leg timing the moment a turning point is judged obscured, rather than continuing to search visually first.
texts_at.2: SP referred to the leg timing and turned onto the next heading about 40 seconds beyond the completion of the leg time. The delay traced to an initial decision to keep searching for the obscured feature through a gap in the cloud before accepting the timing reference. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to accept the leg timing as the primary reference as soon as the turning point is assessed as obscured.
texts_at.3: SP turned to the next point at the completion of the leg time, with the decision reached within about 18 seconds of that point. The small residual came from a last visual check of the gap in the cloud before the timed turn was accepted. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to commit to the timed turn without a final visual check once the point is assessed as obscured.

texts_above.1: SP turned onto the next heading once the IP asked what the leg time was showing, with the turn made about 55 seconds beyond the completion of the leg time. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP referred to the leg timing and turned onto the next heading within about 40 seconds of the completion of the leg time, having accepted the timing reference promptly once the point was judged obscured. Committing to the timed turn without a final visual check would tighten that margin further on the next obscured point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured timed turn decision-making.
texts_above.3: SP turned to the next point at the completion of the leg time whenever the turning point was covered by clouds, with the decision made within about 18 seconds of that point. The technique is already sound; only a gap opening late in the cloud still tempts a further look before the timed turn is accepted. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined timed turn technique.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the cloud covered turning point, briefed the transition to timed navigation before reaching it and turned exactly at the completion of the leg time. The only refinement available was to log the point at which the transition was briefed for the debrief, since the decision itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional timed turn anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to a clock that was never started at the departure point of the leg, did not monitor or control the determined leg durations. SP was unable to state the elapsed or remaining time on any leg and had no groundspeed figure with which to assess the navigation. IP had to run the timing for the remainder of the route and pass the required airspeed corrections.
texts.1: SP, due to leg timings written on the chart but not compared with the clock in flight, monitored the leg durations only when asked. SP produced the elapsed time and the required correction each time after IP requested it, and no independent check was made between prompts. Control of the leg durations existed only through that repeated questioning.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed check omitted at the first half-leg checkpoint, initially had no assessment of the developing timing error. SP reinstated the check at the following checkpoint, computed the groundspeed against the elapsed time and adjusted the airspeed to restore the planned leg duration. Timing control was recovered without any IP input.
texts.3: SP monitored and controlled the determined durations of each leg, starting and stopping the timing at the correct points and checking groundspeed at the planned checkpoints. Airspeed corrections were computed from the elapsed time and applied while the errors were still small. Every leg was completed within the planned duration.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous picture of elapsed time, remaining time and groundspeed for every leg and could state all three on request at any point of the route. Corrections were computed in advance of the checkpoints and applied smoothly, so no leg duration required a late adjustment. Control of the leg timings was precise throughout the navigation.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the leg durations within standards, but the timing was checked only at the turning points and no intermediate groundspeed check was made. The roads seen did not match the charted classification, as only dual lane highways are reliably portrayed, and the built up area had grown well beyond the outline on the chart. SP turned on a false fix, missed the turning point by more than 3 NM and arrived more than 60 seconds off the planned time, and IP had to reestablish the position.

error_modes.label: ANXIETY DISORIENTATION AFTER A MISSING LANDMARK

texts.0: SP, due to anxiety disorientation after the chart to ground method failed to produce an anticipated landmark, treated the missing feature as proof of being lost while the aircraft was still on course. SP abandoned the planned headings and times and wandered while deciding what to do, without checking the clock or reviewing the progress from the last known position. The route error grew beyond 3 NM and beyond 60 seconds and IP had to take over the navigation and restore the aircraft to the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to the same anxiety after an expected landmark did not appear, began to search away from the planned heading instead of continuing on the preplanned heading and time. The reaction to a missing feature was unchanged on the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief loss of confidence when an anticipated landmark was not seen, initially deviated from the planned heading and allowed the error to reach about 1.5 NM and about 45 seconds. SP checked the clock, noted the time, reviewed the progress from the last known position and elected to continue on the preplanned headings and times until the next positive landmark appeared. The navigation was recovered without any IP intervention.
texts.3: SP continued flying the preplanned headings and times when an anticipated landmark failed to appear, recognizing that a missing feature is not by itself evidence of being lost. The clock was checked immediately and the progress from the last known position was reviewed while the aircraft remained on the planned track. The following turning point was made within 1 NM and within 30 seconds of the planned time.

The episode produced negligible effect on the track and on the timing of the navigation.
